lesson.title: Turning Factories into Weapons
lesson.summary: After entering the war, the United States converted its civilian industrial base into the largest war production machine in history, ending the Depression and reshaping the American economy.
lesson.body:
Winning a two-front war meant out-producing Germany and Japan combined, and the U.S. government moved quickly to make that happen. In January 1942, Roosevelt created the War Production Board to direct the conversion of American industry from consumer goods to military supplies. Automobile factories stopped making cars and started making tanks, jeeps, and aircraft engines. Ford's massive Willow Run plant in Michigan, built specifically for the war effort, eventually turned out B-24 Liberator bombers at a pace that stunned observers, sometimes finishing more than one plane an hour at peak production. Shipyards on both coasts used new mass-production techniques to launch cargo ships known as Liberty ships in a matter of days rather than months.

This was a far larger and more centralized mobilization of the economy than anything the New Deal had attempted in peacetime, but it built directly on precedents the New Deal had set. Agencies created to fight the Depression, such as those that had put the federal government in the business of large public works and economic planning, established the idea that Washington could direct economic activity on a massive scale for a national purpose. The war simply raised the scale enormously and gave that planning a single, urgent goal: total military output.

To manage scarce resources at home, the Office of Price Administration rationed goods that were needed for the war effort or in short supply, including gasoline, rubber, sugar, meat, and shoes. Families received ration books with stamps that limited how much of each item they could buy, and posters urged citizens to grow 'victory gardens' and conserve scrap metal, paper, and rubber for recycling into war materials. The government also sold war bonds aggressively, both to finance the war and to soak up consumer spending power at a time when factories were making tanks instead of refrigerators.

The economic effects were dramatic. Unemployment, which had remained stubbornly high through the 1930s despite New Deal programs, essentially disappeared as war industries demanded workers. Federal spending on war production dwarfed anything spent on Depression-era relief programs, and industrial output roughly doubled between 1941 and 1945. The war did what a decade of New Deal policy had not fully managed to do: it ended the Great Depression, though at the cost of turning the nation's factories, and much of daily life, entirely toward the demands of war.
